idiom_name: object with pure methods, or final class taking collaborators as constructor parameters
implementation_notes: Scala 3 makes the choice cheap: an object (or a trait with a companion object) holds the operation as a pure method when there is nothing to inject, and a final class taking its collaborators as constructor parameters is the injected form. The DDD separated interface is optional, so add the trait only where substitution is genuinely needed; Scala's object is a lazily-initialised JVM singleton, which is exactly the 'single instance per execution context' that Evans describes - and exactly why it must stay stateless.
code_sketch:
trait ExchangeRateSource:
  def rateFor(from: Currency, to: Currency): BigDecimal

final class ExchangeService(rates: ExchangeRateSource):   // stateless
  def convert(amount: Money, target: Currency): Money =
    amount.times(rates.rateFor(amount.currency, target)).in(target)
pitfalls: An object is a class-loader-wide singleton: any var inside it is global mutable state shared by every thread.
Initialisation order between objects is lazy and surprising; a service that touches another object during construction can observe uninitialised state.

Implicit/given resolution can silently inject a different instance than intended when two givens of the same type are in scope; prefer explicit constructor parameters for services and keep givens for the tagless-final variant.

variants.name: Tagless-final service (algebra parameterised by an effect)
variants.idiom_name: trait Service[F[_]] + context bounds + given interpreters (Cats Effect IO, Id in tests)
variants.implementation_notes: Express the domain operation as a method on an algebra trait Service[F[_]] whose result type is the effect F, declare the capabilities it needs as context bounds (F[_]: Monad) and supply interpreters as given instances - Scala 3's given/using replaces implicit parameters, and the effect can be Cats Effect IO in production and a pure identity-like effect in tests. This is the functional realization of the same stateless operation: constructor injection becomes context parameters and the service class becomes a trait parameterised by effect, which is worth the abstraction only when the application is already built on an effect system.
variants.code_sketch:
trait Exchange[F[_]]:
  def rateFor(from: Currency, to: Currency): F[BigDecimal]

def convert[F[_]: Monad](amount: Money, target: Currency,
                         ex: Exchange[F]): F[Money] =
  ex.rateFor(amount.currency, target).map(r => amount.times(r).in(target))
pitfalls: Every method of the algebra shares one constraint set, so unrelated capabilities over-constrain every interpreter; keep only genuinely variant operations in the algebra and put the rest in a plain object.
Forgetting to suspend an effect (running a side effect eagerly while building F) breaks the interpreter; effects must be values until run.
Type-class coherence is a convention, not a compiler rule: two given interpreters for the same F type make behaviour depend on import order.
